narrative:
The model estimated a 56.5% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is above the threshold used in this process, your law school application was denied. This does not mean failure is certain; it means the prediction leaned slightly toward risk rather than success.

The strongest factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the third decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile, and this lower standing was the main reason the prediction moved toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year standing—fifth decile versus an accepted average around sixth—was the second-most influential factor, but in this case it pushed toward passing. Your upper-middle family-income bracket, the most common bracket among accepted students, was the third-most influential factor and slightly nudged the prediction toward failure. Other information, such as your LSAT and undergraduate GPA, mattered less than those top three factors.

To respond, ask admissions whether feedback or conditional review is available, and focus on strengthening your LSAT score, which at 35 is below the accepted average of 37.18. Highlight your 3.40 GPA, which is above the accepted average of 3.23, and document any upward academic trend or bar-readiness preparation. Consider retaking the LSAT, meeting with a pre-law advisor, and reapplying after additional preparation rather than treating this prediction as a final verdict.
